plain_title: Constant fear of having a serious illness
one_liner: Being preoccupied with having or getting a serious illness despite few symptoms, either checking constantly or avoiding care.
in_simple_words: Illness anxiety disorder is intense, lasting fear of having or developing a serious illness, when there are few or no physical symptoms, or only mild ones. The person checks their body, researches symptoms, seeks repeated reassurance and tests, or, in the other pattern, avoids doctors entirely out of fear. Reassurance helps for a moment and then the fear returns. It's exhausting, it's very common, and it responds well to CBT.
what_it_can_feel_like: Every headache was a tumour. Every ache was the start of something. I had more scans than my grandmother.
The relief after a normal test lasted about a day. Then I'd find a new symptom.
Therapy taught me that checking was the problem, not the solution.
common_signs: Preoccupation with having or getting a serious illness
Few or mild physical symptoms, or none
High anxiety about health; easily alarmed by bodily sensations
Repeatedly checking the body, researching, or seeking reassurance
Or: avoiding doctors and hospitals out of fear
Lasting six months or more, even if the feared illness changes

myths_vs_facts.fact: The fear is genuine and distressing. Many people with health anxiety are ashamed of it and hide it.

myths_vs_facts.myth: One more test will settle it.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Reassurance and testing feed the cycle. Learning to tolerate uncertainty is what ends it.
Untreated health anxiety damages quality of life, relationships, and finances, and can delay care for real problems.

how_common.plain: Health anxiety affects somewhere between 1 and 5 in 100 adults, with higher rates in people attending medical clinics.
how_common.figure: Estimates range from 1.3% to 10% in the general population; around 3%–8% in medical outpatient settings (DSM-5-TR text and reviews)

what_helps.plain_summary: CBT for health anxiety is the first-line treatment, with strong evidence: it works on the beliefs about symptoms, reduces checking and reassurance-seeking, and builds tolerance of uncertainty. Internet-delivered CBT is effective too. Antidepressants (SSRIs), prescribed and monitored by a doctor, help many people, especially where there's depression. A steady relationship with one doctor who agrees a plan for tests and reviews helps.
evidence_based_options: CBT for health anxiety, in person or online
SSRI antidepressants, prescribed and monitored by a doctor
An agreed plan with one doctor for check-ups and tests
self_help_that_supports_care: Stopping symptom searching and body checking, gradually
Asking loved ones to stop giving reassurance, by agreement
Noticing anxiety's own body symptoms: racing heart, tingling, dizziness
Scheduled 'worry time' instead of all-day worry

when_to_reach_out: If fear of illness is taking up hours of your day, driving repeated tests, or keeping you away from doctors, ask for CBT for health anxiety. Keep one doctor for real medical questions, and let them know about the anxiety too.
is_not: Sensible attention to health, worry while awaiting results, or anxiety with a real diagnosis are not the disorder. Somatic symptom disorder involves significant symptoms; illness anxiety involves few or none. Fear of contamination with rituals is more likely OCD.
hope_note: Health anxiety has one of the best responses to CBT of any condition. People who checked their bodies hourly learn to live without the dread.
